replying_to: Replying to Accurate Word Representations with Universal Visual Guidance
display_title: The idea is interesting, but there are flaws in experiments and model design.

content.title: The idea is interesting, but there are flaws in experiments and model design.
content.review:
1.Objective of the work: This work proposes to integrate external visual knowledge into the contextualized word representations (CWP). The goal is to equip CWP with the ability to disambiguate and make CWP "more contextualized." 

2.Metrits of the paper: Most multimodal researches focus on solving multimodal tasks, like cross-modal retrieval, VQA, etc. In comparison, this paper (along with some others) use multimodal information to address mono-modal tasks (language understanding, NMT). And the proposed method is general that can be applied to many downstream tasks. From this perspective, this paper is interesting and will benefit the community.

3.Concerns:

3.1 One of the authors' major claims/motivation is that their model is better in disambiguating by leveraging word-level multimodal information. But I did not see any analysis or case studies to substantiate this claim (except section 4.3 which we will discuss later). This makes it unclear to me where the gains on NLU and NMT tasks come from. For instance, Table 2 reports a large improvement(>10%) on RTE over BERT, which is impressive. But personally, I didn't find any ambiguous instances in RTE dataset that can be resolved by introducing visual knowledge. 

3.2 Another key concern about the paper is the lack of novelty in the methodology. The proposed method seems like a straightforward extension of [1], with two minor changes: (a) replace the decoder with MLP to solve NLU tasks. (b) consider images on word-level instead of sentence-level (see 3.3 below). The rest of the model is exactly the same as in [1], but this strong connection has not been discussed when describing section 3.2 

3.3 The reason for doing word-level lookup, according to the authors, is that the sentence-level lookup suffers from irrelevant noise. However, by inspecting the examples in Appendix A.1, it seems that although word-level lookup injects more diversity, it also brings more noise. For example, in the second "glass" picture, the glasses is hard to notice. And since the author is using pooled representation from ResNet, the extracted vector can be very noisy (i.e. the extracted features will be related to more "noticeable" objects in the picture like "man", "black suit", rather than the desired "glass"). One possible fix I can imagine is to use visual grounding toolkits like [2] to detect visual objects before feature extraction (as an example, see [3]). 

Also, as reported in Table 3, sentence-level lookup is compatible with the proposed method on WMT'16 EN-RO and even superior on WMT'14 EN-DE, which somehow supports my observation. 

3.4 The results of NLU tasks (Table 2) are encouraging, but there is a substantial lack of details to help appreciate the results. For instance, it's not clear how the NLU model is trained. Did you use pre-trained BERT as your model's text encoder, or train the whole model from scratch? My understanding is that you are using the former approach?

3.5 For Table 1, it seems that only the challenge set was created with ambiguous words, but not the training set. Thus is not clear how the model that is trained on a "not-ambiguous" set learns to disambiguate. My guess is that the training set might also contain some ambiguous sentences. It would be great if the authors can add a few case studies to show how vision can help disambiguate translation. 


4.Other suggestions:

The example in Figure 1 is actually not a very good one. I understand the point the authors try to make here, but use "apple" to represent "iPhone" is kind of far-fetched. 

Typo in page 7. "(described in Section 3 below)" should be above? 



[1] Neural machine translation with universal visual representation. In International Confer- ence on Learning Representations,  Zhuosheng Zhang, Kehai Chen, Rui Wang, Masao Utiyama, Eiichiro Sumita, Zuchao Li, and Hai Zhao. ICLR 2020

[2] A fast and accurate one-stage approach to visual grounding. Zhengyuan Yang, Boqing Gong, Liwei Wang, Wenbing Huang, Dong Yu, and Jiebo Luo. ICCV 2019

[3] A Novel Graph-based Multi-modal Fusion Encoder for Neural Machine Translation. Yongjing Yin, Fandong Meng, Jinsong Su, Chulun Zhou, Zhengyuan Yang, Jie Zhou, Jiebo Luo. ACL 2020

content.title: Thanks for your insightful comments. We added more comparisons and experimental details.
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful review and suggestions. We have revised the paper according to your suggestions. The followings are our responses to specific concerns and questions. 

1. claim/motivation that the model is better in disambiguation.

   Please see our General Response 1.

1. About the novelty.

   Please see our General Response 2. We have rephrased the detailed differences to Zhang et al. (2020) in Section 2.2, and added the connection of the model in Section 3.2.

1. Irrelevant noise.

   We added a comparison by using random images for all our evaluation datasets, as the results shown in Table Tables 2-3. We see that the results would not decay much and even slightly better than the baseline in some small-scale datasets, which indicates that the noise would not be harmful. We added a detailed discussion in Section 4.4 (3), demonstrating that the noise might serve as a kind of regularization. A similar finding was also discussed in Zhang et al. (2020). In our current design, after obtaining the word-image lookup table in pre-processing, each word will be paired with a fixed set of images, which could serve as kind of topic information, or senses, for the corresponding word, where diversity might be more important than the risk of noise, based on our results of the consistent improvements over the baselines in a series of datasets. 

   Yes, using visual grounding toolkits could be beneficial to extract "noticeable" objects. However, they might restrict our model to only model a small set of specific objects instead of using the overall image features to augment the word representations in a more diverse way. 

1. How the NLU model is trained.

   The details are in Section 4.2.1. We use the pre-trained BERT for fine-tuning.

1. Ambiguous words in the training and challenge sets of the English-Hindi dataset.

   Yes, the training set has ambiguous sentences. The difference is that all the challenge sets are created by ambiguous words to evaluate the model performance in terms of ambiguity.

1. The example in Figure 1.

   Thanks for your suggestion, we added another example in the Appendix.

display_title: Interesting concept, but the experimental results are not convincing re: the model is meaningfully integrating visual information.

content.title: Interesting concept, but the experimental results are not convincing re: the model is meaningfully integrating visual information.
content.review:
The authors propose a multimodal model that augments text-only tasks
with visual information at the word level (versus most prior works
which augment at the sentence-level). Specifically, for each token in
an input sentence, a dictionary lookup is performed and several
relevant images are obtained. A joint encoding is computed using a
transformer model, which is evaluated on GLUE and MT tasks. The
authors report modest performance gains when integrating their
multimodal components.

The motivation for this work is strong: it definitely seems like
integrating multimodal information should be helpful for language
understanding tasks: after all, when humans address these tasks, our
reasoning isn't limited to text-only inferences. The model itself is
appropriate, and the idea of retrieving relevant images for text
(though not new) is interesting. The experiments cover an appropriate
swath of language processing tasks.

However, my primary technical concern is that it's difficult to tell
if the performance improvements in MT and NLU are due to the
integration of the multimodal information, or if they are due to some
other factor (hyperparameters, number of parameters, number of model
comparisons, etc.). One missing baseline: the author's model, but
trained with random images retrieved. This baseline would isolate the
impact of semantically meaningful images (versus, e.g., simply having
access to more parameters relative to the baselines). In fact, the
authors NLU BERT baseline, which was trained "without any
modification" from the original procedure, illustrates the amount of
variability one might expect under multiple runs of finetuning BERT
(compare: BERT vs. "baseline" rows in Table 2). Given the small
magnitude of difference in performance, I really would have liked to
have seem some estimate of confidence (e.g., train 5x and report the
mean). Looking in the appendix, I have even more concerns: Table 4
shows that the authors tried 3 versions of their model, and switching
to WWM (vs. base or large) seems to have a much greater impact than
incorporating visual information.

My concern that the performance gains might be due to a factor other
than meaningful semantic integration of visual information is
exacerbated by the lack of error analysis. If the multimodal model
outperforms the single modal one, I would have expected to see an
analysis of the instances for which the multimodal model does better:
where does the visual information help, and does it make sense that it
helps there? The appendix contains some examples of images that are
retrieved, but analyses stop there.

Overall, I think there are some interesting ideas in this work:
augmenting individual tokens (vs. whole sentences) with visual
information is a new-enough idea, and it would be interesting to see
if such an augmentation could help with text-only tasks. However, both
the experimental results and lack of model interpretation lead me to
lead strongly towards rejection at this time: I simply am not
sufficiently convinced that the model is meaningfully integrating
visual information to improve performance. I really do like the idea
of this work, and hope that the authors update with baselines and
analyses (similar to those suggested here) that more directly
interrogate the question of multimodal integration.

Other technical concerns:

- The authors (e.g., in the abstract) claim that pretrained LMs only
  have access to 1 sentence of context. But this isn't the case:
  RoBERTa, for example, is pretrained with 512 token contexts. (see
  S4.2 of the RoBERTa paper)

- I think that presenting the performance of other methods (e.g.,
  MT-DNN, GPT) detracts from the author's point. For these
  experiments, adding in additional baselines seemingly serves almost
  no purpose: the main comparison that "matters" is "baseline"
  vs. "ours". Including, e.g., GPT performance invites the question:
  why wasn't RoBERTa included? Why not T5? Why not other baselines for
  MT that outperform UVR? Simply removing them probably makes the most
  sense. Including the set of baselines that happen to just be
  slightly worse than the author's proposed model seems both
  distracting and misleading to me.


Presentation suggestions:

- There are a few words that seem to overclaim. E.g., in the abstract,
  I think "paradise" could possibly be swapped to something more like
  "performant method"; and, I think "remarkable" could be removed in
  reference to tasks.

- The authors motivate their multimodal model by invoking
  polysemy. But it wasn't clear to me how multimodality explicitly
  solves the single-sentence polysemy problem. Couldn't text
  co-occurences similarly disambiguate? And if the full context is a
  single sentence, is perfect disambiguation even possible?

- "For natural language processing (NLP) tasks, most text is
  unlabeled" --> "For natural language processing (NLP) tasks, most
  text isn't distributed with visual information." ?

- Mikolov et al. 2013 is a good citation for distributed
  representations, but there are many prior works that also deal with
  vector representations for words (e.g., the ones cited in that
  paper).

- The authors tout that their method "does not rely on large-scale
  aligned text-image corpora" but it does: specifically, Multi30K.  I
  understand the distinction: that word-image associations are not
  given explicitly (only sentence-image associations are). But that
  setting has been redily examined in prior work (e.g., Karpathy et
  al. 2014), so this factor doesn't distinguish from prior work.


Karpathy, Andrej, Armand Joulin, and Li F. Fei-Fei. "Deep fragment
embeddings for bidirectional image sentence mapping." Advances in
neural information processing systems. 2014.


~ UPDATE RE: AUTHOR RESPONSE ~

Thank you for adding these baselines! I appreciate your additional experiments, and I did update my score a bit. But, my feelings are summarized in my response to the AC, which I have copied here. I think this work asks interesting questions, and points towards a potentially exciting result. But because the implication of the work /is/ so exciting, I can't bring myself to raise my score without additional concrete evidence the model is really leveraging visual information to solve language-only tasks better. The "Random" baseline is a good step, but, IMO, is still not quite enough. For more about my thoughts:

~

I appreciate that the authors have updated their work to include a "random" baseline (which pairs random images with words) and also a "params" baseline (which has the same number of parameters as the proposed method); these baselines were sorely missing in the original work and I think the updated version is much better. The +VG method indeed seems to outperform these baselines by a small absolute margin. I have updated my score accordingly.

My main concern remains: the claims the authors are making are, in view, still unexplored. The authors hint at "grammatical ambiguity" (which I think is the same as syntactic ambiguity) being resolved via multimodality, but provide no evidence that their model is actually doing that: as I mentioned in my original review, "I would have expected to see an analysis of the instances for which the multimodal model does better: where does the visual information help, and does it make sense that it helps there?"

If indeed the model is leveraging semantically-meaningful visual reference to accomplish language processing tasks (as the authors claim) that would represent a significant advance in vision+language research. But because such an advance would be such a significant milestone, relying solely on accuracy measurements on GLUE/MT tasks doesn't seem sufficient: more concrete evidence that it really is the vision+language grounding that matters is needed beyond high-level intuition. This evidence is not provided in this draft, but I am hopeful the authors can examine more closely why their model is working in future submissions, because I do think this is an interesting direction.
~

display_title: Appreciate your insightful comments. We clarified the technical details and improved the paper presentation accordingly.

content.title: Appreciate your insightful comments. We clarified the technical details and improved the paper presentation accordingly.
content.comment:
Thanks for your recognition of our motivation, idea, and method. We also appreciate your insightful review and suggestions. We have revised the paper according to your suggestions. The followings are our responses to specific concerns and questions. 

1. Factors to the performance gains \& random baseline.

   Yes, we have added the random baseline where each word is randomly paired with images (denoted as *+ Random*). Besides, we also added another baseline that has the same number of parameters as our proposed method by replacing the image features with the default standard normal distribution, which is commonly used in the initialization of the Embedding layer (denoted as *+ Params*), for further comparison with the same number of parameters. 

   The results in Tables 2-3 show that our method also outperforms the augmented baseline and indicate that our method does not simply benefit from more parameters.

2. Concerns about the NLU BERT baseline.

   - "without any modification" means that we did not use any extra tricks such as multi-tasking, and two-stage training: using the trained model from larger-scale MNLI dataset to train the smaller-scale RTE and MRPC datasets, like in some recent studies that involve extra influence factors. Instead, we followed the same fine-tuning procedure as BERT with a single-task setting to focus on our multimodal evaluations. We have removed the "without any modification" to avoid confusion in the new version. 

   - "One might expect under multiple runs of finetuning BERT".

     Yes, our dev results are based on 5 runs with different random seeds. We report the mean on the dev sets in Table 2 in the new version, and add the details in Section 4.2.1. Since the test sets of GLUE are not publicly available, we report the dev results in the paper and put the test results in the Appendix, which are obtained by our best dev model.

   - "Different versions of BERT seem to have a much greater impact than incorporating visual information."

     It is reasonable that these baseline models have a great impact on downstream tasks. They were pre-trained by a huge corpus with a much longer time (even months) than ours, and then fine-tuned on the task datasets. Specifically, the WWM model benefits from a word-level masking strategy during the pre-training. In contrast, our method basically shares the same computation time with the baseline. In terms of the model size, the parameter numbers of BERT  LARGE and BASE are 340M and 110M, respectively. In contrast, our model only introduces around 5M parameters over the NLU baselines. Therefore, the results should not be comparable. Our method is much more light-weight and computation-friendly compared with baselines.

3. Processing sentence of context in PrLMs.

   The description follows the commonly-used terms like "next sentence prediction" (BERT), "sentence order prediction" (ALBERT), etc. In PrLMs, for better understanding, the sentence simply means the input processing unit, though, in practice, it often involves multiple sentences, even a document. To avoid the potential concern, as you mentioned, we have modified the description as "a sequence of text contexts" in the new version.

4. Presenting the performance of other methods (e.g., MT-DNN, GPT) detracts from the author's point.

   Yes, following your suggestion, we have removed all the extra baselines. Meanwhile, we have reorganized Table 2 to present more clear comparisons with different augmented baselines. The results show that our method can yield consistent gains over the baseline.

5. Presentation suggestions.

   Thanks for your suggestions, we have revised the paper accordingly.

display_title: Using paired text-image data improves NLU and NMT tasks; concerns about novelty and presentation

content.title: Using paired text-image data improves NLU and NMT tasks; concerns about novelty and presentation
content.review:
In this work, the authors explore techniques to use multimodal paired image-text data to learn a “image-word dictionary” which can be used to augment text-based embeddings with information derived from images. The authors evaluate the proposed techniques on a number of tasks. The main novelty over the previously published work of Zhang et al. (2020) appears to be the use of sub-words instead of word tokens for some tasks, and the evaluation of the proposed techniques on various NLU tasks.

My main concerns about this work are related to it’s novelty -- in particular, the similarities to the previous work of Zhang et al. (2020); and the presentation of the work -- in particular, the english usage, as well as the fact that many important details are missing or hard to understand (for example, the analysis section). My main comments appear below:

Main comments:
 - The presentation of the paper, and in particular the usage of english makes it somewhat hard to read. I’ve included some examples below, but I would suggest that the authors examine the entire paper and correct similar inconsistencies throughout:
  * Some sentences contain somewhat unusual word choices:
“12 *remarkable* natural language understanding and machine translation tasks”;
“*stiffing* disambiguation” (could the authors clarify what this is); 
“Multimodal information might provide *auxiliary instructions* to help ...”; 
“... we first perform experiments on a disambiguation task as *appetizer* ...”
  * Some sentences contain awkward phrasing: 
“ … therefore, it is essential to release the inconvenient constraint on the annotation prerequisite when applying visual information … “; 
“... so that it easily suffers from the noise of irrelevant images.”
  * Some contain grammatical errors: 
“Meanwhile, multimodality derived from word representations can also be more helpful to provide as *more* images as possible … “ --> “... as many images as possible”; 
“However, these approaches blindly create word vectors without taking into account the shared dependencies and context *in which each word entails*”; 
“... based on the *lingual* corpus”; 
“... which ensures the token overlap with task datasets to the maximum *extend*” --> “... extent”
 - In Section 3.1, the authors mention that they build a word-image dictionary “inspired by Zhang et al. (2020)”. To the best of my understanding, the only difference between the authors’ proposed method and the one described in (Zhang et al., 2020) is that in the present work the authors propose to tokenize the sentence using a “tokenizer that depends on downstream tasks”. In my view, this is not very novel. Also, if this is one of the claims of the paper, then I think then authors should conduct experiments to demonstrate that using sub-word embeddings is indeed better than using word-embeddings as in (Zhang et al., 2020). Does this experiment correspond to the results in Table 3? I would suggest that the authors re-write the paper to more clearly communicate the relationship of the proposed work to the work described in Zhang et al. (2020). 
 - The description of Algorithm 1, and Section 3.1 / 3.2 is not very clear. For example, in Section 3.1, the authors mention that “At the end of processing the whole multimodal corpus, we form a word-image dictionary where each subword contains diverse images sorted by the number of image occurrence, which are later converted to the image representation as visual hints.” I did not follow how this sorting was done. Based on reading (Zhang et al., 2020) I assume that the authors mean that they sort the retrieved images for a new input sentence based on the counts, but I’m not sure if the authors mean something else. Also, even in that setting, I assume that there are many images in the list of retrieved images which have the same count. The authors do not mention how they break ties in this case when sorting the images. Also, a minor point: in the description, the authors use “m” to represent both the number of subwords in the tokenization as well as the number of images that are retrieved (section 3.1 and 3.2) which is a bit confusing.
 - Something that I missed after reading this paper is the difference in the results between the work proposed in this paper by the authors and the previous work of (Zhang et al., 2020) on the NMT tasks (i.e., the results in Table 3). Could the authors clarify what the differences between UVR and “ours” in that table are?
 - In the results reported in Table 2, the authors show results for the proposed method against the Baseline which is described in Section 4.2.1 to be BERT. The table also contains a separate results for BERT from (Devlin et al., 2019). What are the differences between these two systems?
 - The analysis presented in Section 5 is extremely brief, and at least in my view, is not very clear. The graphs in Figure 4 and Figure 5 are not easy to read because it is not clear what the values that correspond to each of the points/bars in the graph are. Also, I did not understand the “Image coverage analysis” based on the description. Finally, the description in the section titled “The influence of images corpus” was extremely brief. Also, I think this analysis would be more interesting if it were conducted on multiple tasks instead of on just the EN-DE task. 
 - The authors mention at the end of section 4.4 that the proposed systems have more parameters than the baselines (6.3%). Given that the gains on some tasks appear to be relatively small over the baseline [example on MNLI and QNLI (0.3% absolute); SNLI (0.2% absolute)] I think it is necessary to conduct experiments with exactly the same number of parameters to demonstrate an improvement. Also, while it is great that the authors conduct significance testing on Table 3, I was wondering if the differences in Table 2 relative to the baseline are significant.”

Minor Comments:
- Section 3.3: Could the authors clarify what they mean by “SAN-based encoder”?
- Section 4.2.1: Please cite (Sennrich et al., 2016) or another appropriate reference for SentencePiece
- A detail which I might have missed was how many images, m, were used as inputs to the “image encoder” in the experiments that appear in Section 4.3 and 4.4

************************
Update after author comments
************************

I appreciate the authors efforts to revise the paper based on the reviewers' comments. In particular, the new experimental baselines address some of the concerns that I and other reviewers raised. However, I still feel that the work feels incremental relative to the previous work of Zhang et al. As I mentioned in the review, I think the work could be significantly strengthened by expanding on the analysis section to demonstrate the benefits of the finer-grained representation. For these reasons, I would like to retain my score as before.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

display_title: Thanks for your valuable review. We added more discussion about the novelty and more experiments and analysis details.

content.title: Thanks for your valuable review. We added more discussion about the novelty and more experiments and analysis details.
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful review and suggestions. We have revised the paper according to your suggestions. The followings are our responses to specific concerns and questions. 

1. The difference between Zhang et al. (2020).

   Please see General Response 2.

1. The sorting in Algorithm 1.

   Yes, you got the point. It is possible that some images have the same count in some rare circumstances, but as discussed in Zhang et al. (2020), the actual content of the image would not affect the performance too much because the diversity of images for each word matters -- the phenomenon is also observed in our comparisons with the *+ Random* baseline as discussed in Section 4.4.

1. The difference in the results between this work and Zhang et al. (2020) in Table 3.

   The results in Table 3 show that our method can achieve much better results than the UVR (Zhang et al., 2020) in the small-scale Multi30K datasets compared with the large-scale WMT datasets. It is reasonable that our method could provide more fine-grained and distinguishable word representations with diverse images for words instead of sentences.

1. What are the differences between the baseline BERT and that from (Devlin et al., 2019)?

   They are our reproduced BERT results and that from (Devlin et al., 2019), respectively. As described in Section 4.2.1, for our baseline, we previously used the public pre-trained weights of BERT and followed the same fine-tuning procedure as BERT without any modification. We use the WWM (whole-word-mask) version of the pre-trained weights as default due to its more stable performance. Detailed comparisons of different pre-trained weights are shown in Appendix A.2. 

   In the new version, we have revised Table 2 following the suggestion from Reviewer 4 to avoid distraction and focus on the main comparison with our baselines.

1. Analysis in Section 5.

   Yes, we have added more detailed discussions in the analysis presented in Section 5. 

1. Experiments with exactly the same number of parameters \& Significance testing in Table 3.

   Yes, we have added the baseline that has the same number of parameters as our proposed method by replacing the image features with the default standard normal distribution, which is commonly used in the initialization of the Embedding layer (denoted as *+ Params*). Our method still outperforms those augmented baselines. The comparison indicates our method does not simply benefit from more parameters.

   Yes, we conducted significance testing in Table 3, which shows that our method outperforms the baseline with $p$-value $<0.05$.

1. Minor Comments.

   "SAN" means "self-attention". According to our preliminary experiments, we set the default maximum number of images $m$ for each word as 5. The details, as well as the citation, have been added in the revised version.

content.title: needs a lot of re-writing
content.review:
This paper proposes a dictionary-based method to enhance word representations with visual knowledge. First, using a paired data of images and captions a dictionary is created. For a downstream task, this dictionary is used to retrieve relevant images for tokens. Text and image representations are fused to enhance each token with a visual context. Experiments on several NLP benchmarks show the effectiveness of the proposed method. I suggest the rejection of this work since 1) it lacks clarity 2) it requires parallel data for images and text but claims otherwise 3) lacks a depth of exploration in terms of generalization.

I list my questions (Q) and suggestions (S) below.

S1 Abstract: 'leveraging the whole sentence-level' delete whole. 'more accurate contextualized' accurate for what please clarify. 'stiffing disambiguation' please define and clarify. 'active polysemy' please define and clarify. 'word-aware' does not make any sense since a representation for each word is induced, please consider changing this term. 'task-specific layer for prediction' prediction for what?, please clarify. '12 remarkable' please delete all instances of remarkable, use more objective language. 'generality' --> 'generalization capability'

S2 Introduction: First sentence, please cite from all decades mentioned. In the second sentence, please cite brown clusters. Define and clarify and give examples for 'stiffing disambiguation over polysemy'. Please delete 'actually'. 'sentence expressions' --> 'sentence meanings'. 'each concerned context' please delete concerned.  'to release the inconvenient constraint' please rephrase. 'irrelevant noise' please delete irrelevant. Please give a convincing example for 'sentence-level clues may not always help word-level disambiguation'. 

S3 Figure1: please find a better example like 'the girl saw the man on the hill with a telescope'

S4 Section 2.1. 'these approaches blindly create word vectors without taking into account the shared dependencies and context in which each word entails' Simply not true. The whole premise of distributed representations based on the idea that shared dependencies and the context determine the meaning of a word. Please be more precise and accurate in your criticism of these methods. 'capturing the semantic, contextual, and syntactic meaning' simply not true -- please support these claims with citations. 

S5 Section 3 Algorithm 1 please define zip()

S6 Figure 2: Following this figure is like following a maze. Please simplify where the flow is natural (left to right or top to down)

S7 Section 4: Please add a random baseline where an image is randomly paired with a word. Please add experiments for other languages such as German and French. 

S8 Table2,3 please add a column for methods using paired vision-and-language data.

S9 Figure4 please clarify which task

Q1 Table2: how do you explain the significant difference between your model and previous models, baseline, and your models on SST2l, MRPC, and QQP?

content.title: Appreciate your insightful comments. We added random baseline and improved the paper representation.
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful review. We have revised the paper according to all the valuable suggestions (S1-S9). The followings are the responses as clarification for some specific suggestions and questions.  

S3: The example in Figure 1.

Thanks for your suggestion. We are afraid that the example is not suitable for our case as it is about sentence-level ambiguity and determined by syntax, which is not the focus of this paper. As discussed in General Response 1, we are motivated to augment the word-level representation with extra multimodal signals instead of directly solving sentence-level ambiguity. However, we agree that it is also an interesting example that might facilitate future research; we provide the example in the Appendix.

S7: Random baseline.

Yes, we have added the random baseline where each word is randomly paired with images (denoted as *+ Random*). The results are shown in Tables 2-3, and we add a more detailed discussion in Section 4.4 (3). The results show that our method also outperforms the augmented baseline.

Concerning "the experiments for other languages such as German and French.", we feel quite confused because we have already reported the experiments for German and French, just following the common practice by focusing on EN-DE and EN-FR like previous studies to make comparisons. However, we further add the results of another two subsets (Multi30K 2016 EN-CS and (Multi30K 2017 MSCOCO EN-DE \& EN-FR) for more complete reference in Table 3. 

S8: Add a column for methods using paired vision-and-language data.

Yes, we have added the multimodal model results in Table 3. Please note that there is no paired vision-and-language data for the GLUE benchmark in Table 2 and WMT datasets in Table 3, so we could not find such models.

Q1: The significant difference between your model and previous models.

They were measured by a significance test. As the performances of baseline systems are already very high, we employ the significance test on the dev set (because the test sets are not publicly available) to statistically validate the experimental results, which is a mathematically defined concept to measure if the gain is substantial at a certain confidence level. It is more convincing than the absolute gains by quantifying the random error. The results show that our model achieves consistent and significant gains over the baseline on most of the datasets with $p$-value $<0.05$.

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
Sincerely appreciate your time and the valuable reviews on improving this work and deeply sorry for the late reply as we are working hard on various experiments as suggested. 

First, we address two general concerns below. 

1. The clarification of the term "disambiguation". 

   The major theme of multimodality is to use different modality sources such as texts and images to get a more distinguished representation, which would be beneficial than learning representations from only one modality. Instead of the linguistic term, "disambiguation" in this paper means a broad kind of practice for more distinguishable representation from diverse input sources, which caters to the theme of representation learning of ICLR. Therefore, we integrate the word embeddings with extra image features to obtain more discriminative representations. Disambiguation serves as a general purpose for better and more distinguishable representation, which is partially alleviated by our carefully designed multimodality solution. In the meantime, our proposed model is surely not to supposed to model all possible ambiguity in representation learning. To avoid the potential of possibly overclaiming the disambiguation, we modify the paper by describing such representations as "more distinguishable representation".

1. About the novelty.

   Compared with Zhang et al. (2020), this paper mainly differs from both sides of motivation and technique. 

   - For the motivation, the lookup table constructed at sentence-level as that in Zhang et al. (2020) would lead to the relatively limited coverage of the related images for each sentence and suffers from noise as well. Unlike previous work that incorporates the visual modality as sentence-level guidance, we propose to leverage word-level multimodal assistance, which offers more accurate means for disambiguation as word-level clues may conveniently help solve sentence-level ambiguity. Meanwhile, multimodality derived from word representations can also be more helpful to provide as many images as possible to alleviate the scarcity of images retrieved for sentences.  
   - Technically, we extend the word embeddings with more discriminative image features, enabling the resultant model to benefit broad NLP tasks more than machine translation as previous work focuses on. Intuitively, our method is more fine-grained which can result in adequate word-image overlap. According to the analysis in Section 5, we see that in most of our datasets, over 50\% tokens have paired images, effectively addressing the drawback of sentence-level method in Zhang et al. (2020) as it is hard to guarantee adequate images for each sentence. Further, the results in Table 3 show that our method is indeed better than the previous methods, especially in the small-scale datasets, indicating that our method would be useful for low-resource scenarios.

As a result, the major contributions of this work are as follows:

1. Instead of retrieving images for each sentence sparsely, this work focuses on word-level modeling by enriching word representations with related images as fine-grained visual hints.
2. The proposed approach does not rely on large-scale aligned text-image corpus and can achieve modest results with only a few seed images.
3. Our method is light-weight and is not limited to specific tasks; it is generally motivated to apply visual guidance to a wide range of NLP tasks and can easily be applied to other NLP models. 

For the other concerns and questions, please see the point-to-point response below.
